527: Principal component analysis replaces a large set of correlated traits with a small number of new axes, each a weighted combination of the original traits. The first axis captures as much of the variation as possible, the second as much of the residual variation as possible, and so on. The value of the method lies in rendering a large table interpretable as a figure. Abdelsalam et al. (2025) applied it comparably to rice quality data.
528: Every parameter was first standardised to a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. This step was necessary because the traits are expressed in widely disparate units; without it, the traits of larger numerical magnitude would have dominated the outcome merely by virtue of that magnitude.
529: Six components returned eigenvalues exceeding unity and together accounted for 83.82% of the variation, the first two accounting for slightly more than half. The scree plot in Figure 2 exhibits a sharp inflexion after the second component, the customary indication that the first two carry the greater part of the informative variation.
530: The first component constitutes a storage axis, loading positively on aroma, antioxidant capacity, total phenol, fat, total flavonoid and soluble protein, and negatively on amylose and total colour difference. This axis emerges because storage displaces many traits simultaneously and in a consistent direction: every trait declining during storage loads positively and every trait rising loads negatively. Reading the biplot in Figure 3 from right to left is therefore equivalent to reading the storage period from fresh paddy to twelve months.
531: The second component constitutes principally a varietal axis, loading positively on phytic acid, iron and lightness, and negatively on head rice recovery, ash and amylose. The probable basis is grain anatomy: phytic acid and iron reside largely in the bran and embryo, whereas head rice recovery is contingent upon the density and vitreousness of the endosperm. Landraces differ in the balance between these tissues, so that a single axis separates them.
532: The third component separated the minerals from the remaining characters, loading positively on zinc and copper and negatively on manganese. Since storage exerted no effect on any mineral, this component evidently captures differences between sites in soil mineral supply, which accords with Li et al. (2018) on the influence of growing area upon grain composition.
533: The biplot in Figure 3 renders the structure readily interpretable. The twelve points of the pigmented landrace cluster together on one side, apart from the remainder. Within each landrace the four storage points run in sequence across the plot, the length of that trajectory indicating the magnitude of change in the landrace. Co-directional vectors denote traits that rise and fall together; opposed vectors denote traits that move inversely; and orthogonal vectors denote traits that vary independently, which is why the phytic acid vector lies across the aroma and phenolic group.
534: The practical value lies in the reduction of twenty three determinations to two interpretable dimensions. A treatment may be located on the plot and its entire quality profile read at a glance.
540: Cluster analysis groups treatments according to their similarity across all the traits simultaneously. Ward's method was applied to the standardised data; it amalgamates the two most similar groups at each step and constructs a tree, presented as the dendrogram in Figure 4. The height at which two branches join indicates the extent of their dissimilarity. The cophenetic correlation was 0.503, a moderate value, so that the tree affords a fair though not exact representation of the distances.
541: Cutting the tree into four groups yielded clusters of twelve, four, seven and thirteen treatments. The grouping followed the landrace far more closely than either site or storage period.
542: The first cluster comprised all twelve treatments of the pigmented landrace and nothing further, no treatment of that landrace falling outside it. This cluster led for aroma, phenol, antioxidant capacity, head rice recovery and hulling, and carried the least phytic acid. It separates so cleanly because a pigmented husk and a thicker bran influence many traits simultaneously and in the same direction. Zhang et al. (2010) and Shao et al. (2014) demonstrated how substantial a proportion of the phenolic and antioxidant load of rice resides in those tissues.
543: The second cluster comprised only four treatments, all of one landrace from one site. It stood apart on mineral content rather than on any other attribute, carrying much the greatest quantity of zinc, ash and copper. The probable explanation is soil, since zinc availability to rice depends strongly upon soil reaction, phosphorus status and the duration for which the field remains flooded. This cluster constitutes the clearest confirmation of the location and variety interactions reported throughout this chapter.
544: The third cluster comprised the intermediate and later storage samples of the two non-pigmented landraces, predominantly from one site. This is the deteriorated group, returning the lowest aroma, phenol, antioxidant capacity and ash. It illustrates the outcome where a landrace of only moderate quality is grown at the weakest site and subsequently held for a protracted period.
545: The fourth cluster comprised the fresh and early-stored samples of the same two landraces. It led for phytic acid and iron and was intermediate for most other traits.
546: Three inferences follow. First, landrace constituted the strongest single determinant of overall quality, since the pigmented landrace separated from the others before any further division appeared in the tree. Second, storage was the next strongest, since within the other two landraces the fresh samples separated from the late ones. Third, growing site counted for least overall, yet proved decisive in a single case, where one landrace at one site resolved apart on its mineral content. Abdelsalam et al. (2025) similarly found clustering to separate rice cultivars principally on genotype, with the environment acting upon particular traits.
551: This experiment was designed to disentangle three influences upon the grain quality of the traditional aromatic rices of West Bengal: growing site, landrace and duration of post-harvest storage. Thirty-eight parameters were recorded, three landraces from three locations being evaluated at four storage intervals over two seasons. The location effect was significant for all twenty-three parameters in which storage was assayed, the varietal effect for all twenty-three, and the storage effect for nineteen. The location by variety interaction attained significance for twenty-one parameters and the three-factor interaction for fifteen. Quality in these landraces is therefore not the property of any single factor.
553: Birbhum and Howrah returned the best milling percentage, head rice recovery, total starch, total phenol, total flavonoid, antioxidant capacity, iron, manganese and aroma. Nadia returned the best hulling, soluble protein, fat, ash, moisture retention, copper and zinc, together with the lowest phytic acid. Purba Bardhaman was the weakest location for most attributes determining nutritional value, although it returned the highest amylose and the brightest grain. The growing environment appears to operate by two routes, namely the weather prevailing during grain filling and the mineral status of the soil, neither of which dominated.
555: Kalojira emerged as the outstanding landrace, leading for hulling, milling, head rice recovery, total starch, amylose, fat, ash, aroma, total phenol, total flavonoid and antioxidant capacity, and carrying the least phytic acid. Its small dense kernel, tight pigmented husk and proportionately thicker bran account for the greater part of this advantage. Gobindabhog was superior for soluble protein, grain shape, iron and thirteen of the fifteen amino acids, and is therefore the preferable choice where protein quality or grain iron is the objective. Radhunipagal led for zinc alone and was the poorest performer for the majority of milling and nutritional attributes.
557: Storage acted upon quality in two opposing directions simultaneously, and this constitutes the central finding of the experiment. Milling behaviour improved as the grain aged, head rice recovery gaining 2.14 percentage points by eight months and milling percentage peaking at four months, while amylose rose by 12.8% over the year, displacing the highest landrace into the next cooking-quality class. Against these gains, aroma declined by 31.7%, soluble protein by 41.4%, fat by 31.3%, total phenol by 52.4%, total flavonoid by 37.3% and antioxidant capacity by 62.7%.
558: Two results run counter to the general decline, and both are favourable. Grain concentrations of copper, iron, zinc and manganese registered no change during storage, while phytic acid declined by 40.0%. Since phytic acid is the constituent impeding absorption of iron and zinc, the balance between them improved progressively, and aged grain should therefore release its minerals more readily than fresh grain notwithstanding that it contains no greater quantity of them.
560: The interactions yield three inferences that the main effects alone would conceal. First, for the milling traits and for aroma the order of the landraces was conserved at every location, so that the choice of landrace may be made once for the whole of West Bengal. Second, for soluble protein, ash and all four minerals the order varied from location to location, so that no landrace can be recommended for these traits without specification of the district. Third, for aroma, fat and amylose all three landraces changed at nearly identical rates during storage, which implies that a single storage regime will serve all of them.
562: The three multivariate analyses corresponded with one another and with the analysis of variance. Correlation identified one tightly associated complex of desirable traits, namely aroma, fat, phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant capacity and soluble protein, which decline in concert and against which amylose moves inversely. Principal component analysis reduced twenty-three parameters to two interpretable dimensions accounting together for slightly more than half the variation, the first constituting a storage axis and the second a varietal axis. Cluster analysis resolved all twelve Kalojira treatments into a single group before any other division appeared in the tree. Landrace is therefore the strongest single determinant of overall quality, followed by storage, with location counting for least except in one striking instance.
564: Four recommendations follow from these results. Kalojira should be preferred where aroma, phenolic content and milling outturn are the objectives, and Gobindabhog where protein quality or grain iron is of greater consequence. A storage period of four to eight months represents the optimal compromise, since within that window the greater part of the milling gain conferred by ageing has been realised while the loss of aroma and bioactive compounds remains moderate. Aromatic rice held beyond eight months under ambient conditions forfeits much of the fragrance and antioxidant value for which it commands a premium, and none of it is recoverable. Where protracted holding is unavoidable, cool storage merits consideration, since temperature rather than time governs the rate of these losses.
566: Three limitations should be stated plainly. The amino acid profile was determined on freshly harvested grain alone, so that no conclusion is drawn regarding the effect of storage upon amino acids. The multivariate analyses were based on treatment means rather than individual replicate values; the coefficients therefore describe the covariation of treatment means and do not constitute estimates of correlation among individual observations. Two observations lie far outside the remainder of the data and should be verified against the raw records before the tables are finalised: the length to breadth ratio of Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman at eight months, which fell below unity, and the near-absence of cysteine and tyrosine in Radhunipagal, which is more likely a failure of detection than a genuine absence.
568: The quality of the traditional aromatic rices of West Bengal is governed jointly by landrace, growing location and storage period, the three acting in conjunction rather than independently. Among the landraces examined, Kalojira is the superior all-round choice, combining better milling outturn with the highest aroma and the greatest phenolic and antioxidant content. Storage improves milling behaviour and reduces phytic acid, but at the cost of severe and irreversible losses of aroma, extractable protein, lipid and antioxidant capacity; a holding period of four to eight months reconciles these opposing trends. One wider implication follows: the premium attaching to these landraces rests upon the very attributes that are lost most rapidly in store, so that its realisation depends upon the marketing chain and not upon the breeding programme alone.
